106.title: Sitting between
106.hook: a short sitting between prostrations, asking forgiveness
106.howItsDone: Between the two prostrations of each unit, Muslims sit briefly and still, commonly saying rabbi ighfir li, my Lord, forgive me, or a longer supplication for mercy, guidance, well-being and provision.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sujud, the prostration, forehead on the ground. Your line was closest when lowest. When you felt small, did you hear it as close? Day one hundred six.

Think of the smallest pauses in your day. The second after a door shuts. The breath between two sentences in a hard conversation. The red light before it turns green. We usually rush through them, or fill them with a phone. In the prayer, there's one of these tiny pauses built in on purpose. The forehead comes up from the floor. The person sits back on their heels. And for a few seconds, before going down again, they sit, still, and say something short. It would be easy to skip. The Prophet ﷺ never did. Today: sitting between.
screen: `THE SMALLEST PAUSES.` → `UP FROM THE FLOOR.` → `A FEW SECONDS, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: The sitting is often called jalsa, just a sitting, from the everyday word for sitting down. Every unit of prayer has two prostrations, and between them the person rises with Allahu akbar and sits, usually on the left foot with the right foot upright, hands resting on the thighs. And what do they say? A hadith in the Sunan, from the companion Hudhayfah, reports the Prophet saying here: rabbi ighfir li, rabbi ighfir li. My Lord, forgive me. My Lord, forgive me. That's it. Another report, from Ibn Abbas, gives a longer line: asking God to forgive, to have mercy, to guide, to give well-being, and to provide. Five things in one breath. Either one is said quietly, then Allahu akbar, and back down to the floor. Now the surprising part. You'd think such a short moment would be hurried. A companion named Anas, in Bukhari, said the Prophet would sit between the two prostrations so long that someone would say, he's forgotten. He hadn't. He was just staying there. The hadith of the man who prayed too fast, the one we've met twice now, includes this too: sit until you're at rest in your sitting. So the pause isn't empty space between two important things. It's its own small place. Down to the floor, closest to God. Then up, sitting, and the first thing said is: forgive me. Then down again. There's a rhythm in it, like breathing. Low, then a breath between, then low again.
screen: `JALSA — JUST A SITTING.` · `MY LORD, FORGIVE ME.` · `SO LONG THEY THOUGHT HE'D FORGOTTEN.` · `SIT UNTIL YOU'RE AT REST.` · then, large: `LOW, A BREATH, LOW AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit, breathe, ask once. Sit back, on your heels if that's comfortable, or in a chair with your hands resting on your thighs. Let one breath come in and go out without doing anything. Then, if you pray, say it once, quietly: rabbi ighfir li, my Lord, forgive me. If you don't, just think of one thing you'd like to be let off for, and hold it lightly. Then stay seated, and let the pause be long. The bell holds the time.
Jalsa. The short sitting between the two prostrations, where the words are: my Lord, forgive me. Today's word.
Your line: a breath between. Pick one small pause today, a red light or a closing door, and don't fill it. Let it be a breath between. Day one hundred six.

107.title: The testimony in the sitting
107.hook: the finger raised, the greeting on the Prophet ﷺ and the righteous
107.carry: peace on us and the good
107.howItsDone: After every second unit and at the end of each prayer, Muslims sit and recite the tashahhud, beginning at-tahiyyatu lillah and ending with the testimony of faith, raising the right index finger as they bear witness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jalsa, the short sitting between prostrations. Your line was a breath between. Did you let one small pause stay empty? Day one hundred seven.

Picture someone teaching you something so important they hold your hand while they do it. Not a handshake. Your hand held between both of theirs, the way a grandparent holds a child's hand to show them how to write a letter. A companion named Ibn Mas'ud said that's how the Prophet ﷺ taught him today's words: his hand between the Prophet's two palms, the way he'd teach a chapter of the Qur'an. At the end of every second unit of prayer, and at the very end, the person sits, and says these words, and near the end, lifts one finger. Today: the testimony in the sitting.
screen: `A HAND HELD BETWEEN TWO PALMS.` → `TAUGHT LIKE A SURAH.` → `ONE FINGER RAISED.`

segments.voice: It's called tashahhud, from the root for witnessing, because it ends with the testimony: I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger. As the person says it, the index finger of the right hand is raised, pointing to the one God. The schools differ on exactly when to raise it and whether to move it. But the witness comes at the end. It begins with a greeting. And there's a story, in Bukhari, about how it came to be. Ibn Mas'ud said that early on, the companions would say in the sitting: peace be on Allah, peace on Jibril, peace on Mika'il, peace on so-and-so. The Prophet turned to them and said: don't say peace be on Allah, for Allah is Himself the Peace. Say instead: at-tahiyyatu lillah, all greetings are for Allah, and the prayers and the good things. Peace be on you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings. Peace be on us and on the righteous servants of Allah. And then he added something wonderful. When you say that, he said, it reaches every righteous servant in the heavens and on the earth. Think about what that means. Every Muslim, in every prayer, several times a day, sends peace to every righteous servant of God, in the heavens and on the earth. Not just their friends. Not just their community. Every righteous servant, anywhere. The prayer, sitting on the floor of one small room, reaches out to all of them.
screen: `TASHAHHUD — FROM WITNESSING.` · `DON'T SAY PEACE ON ALLAH.` · `ALL GREETINGS ARE FOR ALLAH.` · `IT REACHES EVERY RIGHTEOUS SERVANT.` · then, large: `PEACE ON US AND THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn the first line. Sit comfortably, hands resting on your thighs. Say it slowly, three times: at-tahiyyatu lillah. All greetings are for Allah. Then, if you pray, you can go on: was-salawatu wat-tayyibat, and the prayers and the good things. If you don't, just hold the image: from where you're sitting, peace going out to every good person, everywhere. Pick one of them you know by name, and hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Tashahhud. The testimony in the sitting: greetings to Allah, peace on the Prophet, on us and on the righteous, then the witness, finger raised. Today's word.
Your line: peace on us and the good. Today, think of one good person you'll never meet, somewhere in the world, and send them peace in your head. Day one hundred seven.

108.title: The peace to both sides
108.hook: turn right, then left: peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah
108.howItsDone: Muslims end every prayer by turning the head to the right and then to the left, saying as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah each time, greeting the angels and the worshippers on either side.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tashahhud, the testimony in the sitting, peace sent to every righteous servant. Your line was peace on us and the good. Did you send peace to someone you'll never meet? Day one hundred eight.
screen: `TASHAHHUD — PEACE ON US AND THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: How do you end a phone call with someone you love? Not just click. You say bye, and bye, and okay, bye, love you, bye. Endings matter. They tell the other person how you're leaving. Now, the prayer. The door closed behind you at the start, with Allahu akbar. For a few minutes you've been somewhere else: standing, bowing, on the floor, sitting. And now you have to come back into the room. How do you walk out of a conversation with God? Today: the peace to both sides.
screen: `OKAY, BYE, LOVE YOU, BYE.` → `ENDINGS MATTER.` → `HOW DO YOU WALK BACK OUT?`

segments.voice: The ending is called taslim, from the same root as salaam, the very first word on this path. In the most common form, at the end of the last sitting, the person turns the head to the right and says: as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah. Peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah. Then to the left, and says it again. Remember the hadith from day one hundred one: the prayer's opening is the takbir, and its closing is the salam, the taslim. The door that closed with Allahu akbar opens again with peace. Who is the greeting for? The scholars give a few answers. The angels, whom the tradition places on the right and left of every person. The people praying beside you in the line. Muslims everywhere. The words are plural, you all, so there's room for all of them. There's a small story in Sahih Muslim that shows how ordinary it's meant to be. A companion named Jabir said that when they prayed with the Prophet ﷺ, they used to wave their hands at the salam, to one side and the other. The Prophet asked why they were waving like restless horses flicking their tails, and told them it was enough to rest the hand on the thigh and give the greeting to your brother on your right and on your left. Just turn your face, and wish peace to the person next to you. That's the last act of the prayer. It doesn't end with a request, or a flourish. It ends with you looking at the people beside you and wishing them peace and mercy.
screen: `TASLIM — FROM THE ROOT OF SALAAM.` · `RIGHT, THEN LEFT.` · `ITS CLOSING IS THE TASLIM.` · `NO NEED TO WAVE.` · then, large: `PEACE TO THE PERSON BESIDE YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn right and left. Sit comfortably, hands resting on your thighs. Take a breath. Turn your head slowly to the right, as far as is comfortable, and if you pray, say: as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah. If not, just think of whoever is on that side of you, in the next room, the next house, the next city, and wish them well. Then turn slowly to the left, and do the same. Come back to center, and sit. The bell holds the time.
Taslim. The closing of the prayer: peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah, turning right, then left. Today's word.
Your line: peace, both ways. The next time you leave a room, a call or a conversation today, leave it the way the prayer does: with a word of peace for whoever's there. Day one hundred eight.

109.title: Counting the units
109.hook: two at dawn, four, four, three at sunset, four at night
109.howItsDone: Muslims pray seventeen obligatory rak'ahs a day: two at fajr, four at dhuhr, four at asr, three at maghrib and four at isha, and travelers commonly shorten the four-rak'ah prayers to two.

segments.voice: Yesterday: taslim, the closing, right, then left. Your line was peace, both ways. Did you leave a room or a call with a word of peace? Day one hundred nine.

Some things you learn as a rhythm before you learn them as facts. The number of days in the months: thirty days has September. A phone number sung in an old commercial. Muslim children often learn the prayers the same way, as a string of numbers they can say in one breath: two, four, four, three, four. It sounds like a code. It's actually a map of the whole day. And each of those numbers counts one thing: a unit of the prayer. You've learned every piece of it this week. Today: how the pieces add up.
screen: `THIRTY DAYS HAS SEPTEMBER.` → `TWO, FOUR, FOUR, THREE, FOUR.` → `A MAP OF THE DAY.`

segments.voice: The unit is called a rak'ah, from the same root as ruku', the bow. One rak'ah is one full cycle: standing and reciting, the bow, rising, two prostrations with the sitting between. Everything you've learned since day one hundred one, in order, is one rak'ah. The daily prayers are built out of them. Fajr, at dawn: two. Dhuhr, midday: four. Asr, afternoon: four. Maghrib, sunset: three. Isha, night: four. Seventeen in all, every day. After every second rak'ah, the person sits for the tashahhud; in the last one, they add the taslim. So a four-rak'ah prayer has a sitting in the middle and one at the end. Why these numbers? Nobody gives a reason from logic. They come from how the Prophet ﷺ prayed, and the tradition keeps them as he did. But there is a story about them. Aisha, his wife, said in a hadith in Bukhari that the prayer was first made obligatory as two rak'ahs each. Then the traveler's prayer was left at two, and the prayer at home was increased. That's why, to this day, a traveler shortens the fours to two. The Qur'an gives the permission, in Surah an-Nisa: no sin in shortening the prayer on a journey. The dawn prayer stays two. The sunset prayer stays three. So the numbers carry a little history in them. Two was the original shape. The day's middle prayers grew. And when you're on the road, the prayer shrinks back to fit you.
screen: `RAK'AH — ONE FULL CYCLE.` · `SEVENTEEN, EVERY DAY.` · `FIRST, TWO EACH.` · `ON THE ROAD, FOUR BECOMES TWO.` · then, large: `TWO, FOUR, FOUR, THREE, FOUR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count on your fingers once. Hold up your hand. Thumb: fajr, two. Index finger: dhuhr, four. Middle finger: asr, four. Ring finger: maghrib, three. Little finger: isha, four. Say it through slowly, then say just the numbers, two, four, four, three, four. Then let your hand rest, and picture one whole rak'ah from standing to the second prostration, in your mind, slowly. If you pray, you know where you'll be at the next one. The bell holds the time.
Rak'ah. One unit of prayer, from standing to the second prostration; seventeen of them every day. Today's word.
Your line: two, four, four, three, four. Say it once at each meal today, and see if it sticks by tonight. Day one hundred nine.

110.title: Different hands, same prayer
110.hook: schools differ on hand placement and small details, and all are valid within the tradition
110.howItsDone: Most Muslims pray according to one school of law, usually the one of their family or region, and pray side by side in the mosque with people who hold their hands, say amin or raise their hands a little differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rak'ah, one full unit of prayer, seventeen a day. Your line was two, four, four, three, four. Did it stick by tonight? Day one hundred ten.

Stand at the back of a big mosque during Friday prayer and look down the line. The man on the left has his hands folded low, below the navel. The one next to him, higher, on the chest. The one next to him has his arms hanging straight at his sides. At the end of the Fatiha, some say amin out loud; some whisper it. A newcomer might think half the room is doing it wrong. Nobody in the line thinks so. They're shoulder to shoulder, and they bow at the same moment. Today: different hands, same prayer.
screen: `HANDS LOW, HANDS HIGH, ARMS DOWN.` → `AMIN ALOUD, AMIN WHISPERED.` → `THEY BOW AT THE SAME MOMENT.`

segments.voice: The word is madhhab, a school of law. Literally it means a way of going, the road someone takes. In the first centuries of Islam, scholars in different cities worked out how to follow the Qur'an and the Prophet's ﷺ example in daily life, and the ones whose methods lasted became schools. Among Sunni Muslims there are four, each named after a scholar: Abu Hanifa in Iraq, Malik in Medina, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Most Shia Muslims follow the Ja'fari school, named after Ja'far al-Sadiq. Why do they differ on something as simple as hands? Because the reports differ. Companions saw the Prophet pray over years, in different places, and remembered different details. So the Hanafi school commonly teaches hands folded below the navel; the Shafi'i, above the navel, below the chest; many Malikis and Ja'faris leave the arms at the sides. Each has its reasons, going back to a report. There's a well-known story about Imam Malik. A caliph, the story goes, wanted to make Malik's book, the Muwatta, the law for the whole empire. Malik said no. The companions, he said, had spread out to different lands, and each land had its own knowledge from them. Leave people with what they have. People sometimes quote a saying, the differing of my community is a mercy. Scholars note it isn't a reliable hadith. But the attitude runs deep: within the tradition, all four Sunni schools are considered valid, and a Muslim can pray behind someone of another school. The details differ. The prayer is one.
screen: `MADHHAB — A WAY OF GOING.` · `FOUR SUNNI SCHOOLS, AND THE JA'FARI.` · `THE REPORTS DIFFER.` · `MALIK SAID: LEAVE PEOPLE BE.` · then, large: `THE DETAILS DIFFER. THE PRAYER IS ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch two people pray differently, calmly. If you can, find a short video of a prayer, or picture the line in that mosque. Look at the hands. Low, high, at the sides. Notice if anything in you wants to decide who's right. Let that go. Then stand, and try each yourself for one breath: hands low, hands high, arms hanging. Notice the prayer doesn't change. If you pray, you already know your own way; just hold it gently. The bell holds the time.
Madhhab. A school of Islamic law, a way of going; four Sunni schools and the Ja'fari, one prayer. Today's word.
Your line: many hands, one prayer. Today, when someone does a familiar thing a little differently from you, notice what's the same underneath. Day one hundred ten.

111.title: When you can't stand
111.hook: you pray sitting, lying, or by signs; the prayer bends to the body
111.howItsDone: Muslims who can't stand pray sitting, often on a chair, leaning forward for the bow and a little further for the prostration; those who can't sit pray lying on their side or back, using signs with the head or eyes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: madhhab, the schools of law, hands low, high or at the sides. Your line was many hands, one prayer. Did you notice what was the same underneath a difference? Day one hundred eleven.

Walk into almost any mosque today and look along the back wall. There's a row of plastic chairs. An older man sits in one, and when the line bows, he leans forward from his seat. When they go down to the floor, he leans a little further. Nobody looks twice. Across town, in a hospital bed, a woman who can't sit up at all moves her eyes and her lips through the same prayer. For ten days now we've been learning how the body stands, bows and falls to the ground. So what happens when the body can't? Today: when you can't stand.
screen: `A ROW OF CHAIRS AT THE BACK.` → `A HOSPITAL BED.` → `WHEN THE BODY CAN'T.`

segments.voice: There's a short hadith in Bukhari that answers it. A companion named Imran ibn Husayn had a painful illness and asked the Prophet ﷺ how to pray. The answer was three lines. Pray standing. If you can't, then sitting. If you can't, then on your side. That's the whole ladder. Scholars filled in the rest: if you can't bow or prostrate, you make the movements with signs, leaning or nodding, a little lower for the prostration than for the bow. If you can't move at all, with your eyes, or in your heart. The prayer keeps going; it just gets smaller to fit. And the Prophet himself did this. When he fell from a horse and hurt his side, he prayed sitting, and in his last illness he prayed sitting, too. The principle underneath it is one of the best-known lines in the Qur'an, from the end of Surah al-Baqarah, in Pickthall's words: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." Scope: what it can hold. The prayer is an obligation, and it's one that bends to the person. It's the same with the washing, which becomes tayammum without water, and the four rak'ahs that become two on a journey. And the same with the fast, as we'll see. Here's what's quietly moving about it. The prayer isn't only for the strong, the flexible, the young. The man in the plastic chair isn't praying a lesser prayer. In the tradition, he's doing exactly what's asked of him. The prayer fits him.
screen: `STANDING. SITTING. ON YOUR SIDE.` · `BY SIGNS, OR WITH THE EYES.` · `THE PROPHET PRAYED SITTING TOO.` · `NOT BEYOND ITS SCOPE.` · then, large: `THE PRAYER FITS THE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one prayer's shape, sitting. Stay in your chair. Raise your hands for the opening, then rest them. Sit tall for the standing. For the bow, lean forward from the hips a little. Come back up. For the prostration, lean a little further, lower than the bow. Sit back. Lean again. Sit. Move slowly, like someone who's doing it because this is what the body allows. If you pray, you can say the words as you go. The bell holds the time.
When you can't stand. Pray sitting; if you can't, on your side; if you can't, by signs. The prayer bends to the body. Today's word.
Your line: the prayer fits you. Today, if you're tempted to skip something good because you can't do the full version, do the smaller one. Day one hundred eleven.

fork.setup: you're Imran ibn Husayn, ill and in pain, and you ask the Prophet ﷺ how to pray. what does he say?
options: standing; if you can't, sitting; if you can't, on your side
fork.reveal: three lines in Bukhari: pray standing, if you can't then sitting, if you can't then on your side. the prayer bends to the body.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslim prayer needs a healthy, flexible body.
what it means: the prayer steps down to sitting, lying or signs; it bends to the body.
what a scholar hears: Imran ibn Husayn's hadith (Bukhari 1117) and the principle of 2:286, the same logic as tayammum and shortening on a journey.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:286
Sahih al-Bukhari 1117 (Imran ibn Husayn: standing, sitting, on your side)
Sahih al-Bukhari 378 and 688 (the Prophet praying sitting after his fall, and in his last illness)

112.title: One whole prayer
112.hook: putting it together: dawn prayer, two units, start to finish
112.howItsDone: The dawn prayer, fajr, is two rak'ahs prayed between first light and sunrise, recited aloud when leading, and many Muslims precede it with two voluntary rak'ahs, often at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday: when you can't stand, the prayer bends to the body. Your line was the prayer fits you. Did you do the smaller version of something, instead of skipping it? Day one hundred twelve.

Two weeks ago we started with the intention. Since then: cleanness, a direction, five times, two words that open the door, the standing, the bow, the rising, the prostration, the sitting between, the testimony, the peace to both sides, the count, the schools, and the chair at the back. Fifteen pieces, one a day, counting the intention. It's like learning a song one bar at a time. Today you hear it played through, once, from the first note to the last. The shortest of the five: dawn, two units. Today: one whole prayer.
screen: `FIFTEEN PIECES, ONE A DAY.` → `ONE BAR AT A TIME.` → `NOW PLAYED THROUGH.`

segments.voice: It's still dark. The sky is only beginning to gray. That's fajr's time. The person has made wudu, is on a clean spot, facing the qiblah. In the heart, the intention: two rak'ahs of the dawn prayer. Hands rise. Allahu akbar. The door closes behind. Hands fold, eyes down. The Fatiha, then a short surah, recited aloud if leading, because the dawn prayer is one of the spoken ones. Allahu akbar, and the bow: glory to my Lord the Great, three times, settled. Rising: Allah hears whoever praises Him. Our Lord, and to You be the praise. Allahu akbar, and down: forehead, nose, hands, knees, toes. Glory to my Lord the Most High. Up to sit: my Lord, forgive me. Down again, the second prostration. That's one rak'ah. Allahu akbar, and up to stand again, and the whole cycle repeats: Fatiha, a surah, bow, rise, prostrate, sit, prostrate. Then, instead of standing, the person stays seated. The tashahhud: all greetings are for Allah, peace on the Prophet ﷺ, peace on us and the righteous, finger raised for the witness. Then blessings on the Prophet and on Ibrahim. Then right: as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah. Left: the same. And it's over. Five minutes, maybe less. And many Muslims pray two more voluntary rak'ahs just before this one, which the Prophet said, in Sahih Muslim, are better than the world and everything in it. The whole thing. Every piece you've learned, in order, before the sun is up.
screen: `STILL DARK. WUDU. FACING THE QIBLAH.` · `STAND, BOW, RISE, PROSTRATE, SIT.` · `ONCE MORE, THEN THE TESTIMONY.` · `PEACE, RIGHT AND LEFT.` · then, large: `EVERY PIECE, IN ORDER, BEFORE SUNRISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: two rak'ahs. If you pray, pray the two now, slowly, the way you've learned them, noticing each piece as it passes. If you don't, walk through the shape, standing or in your chair, without words: raise your hands, stand, bow, rise, go down or lean, sit, go down again. Then once more. Then sit, and turn your head right, and left. Two cycles. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
One whole prayer. Fajr, two rak'ahs: takbir to taslim, every piece in order. Today's word, and the end of the prayer, step by step.
Your line: the whole thing. Tomorrow at dawn, if you're awake, notice the gray sky, and know that somewhere a whole prayer is being prayed under it. Tomorrow, the fingers. Day one hundred twelve.

match.prompt: which words, which moment — tap the pairs.
pairs: glory to my Lord the Great
peace, to the right and left

myth: the dawn prayer is four rak'ahs
fajr is two rak'ahs, the shortest of the five.
the Prophet ﷺ said the two voluntary rak'ahs before fajr are better than the world
better than the world and everything in it (Sahih Muslim).
the dawn prayer is recited silently
it's one of the spoken prayers; the one leading recites aloud.

fork.setup: you've finished the second prostration of the first rak'ah of fajr. what comes next?
options: sit for the tashahhud and end
stand up for the second rak'ah
fork.reveal: you stand with Allahu akbar and repeat the whole cycle; the tashahhud and the peace come after the second rak'ah.

original.note: Arabic: the dawn prayer. fajr means dawn, the first break of light.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslim prayer is a long, complicated ritual.
what it means: the whole dawn prayer is two rak'ahs, takbir to taslim, about five minutes.
what a scholar hears: the pillars in order, the jahri (aloud) recitation at fajr, and Muslim 725 on the two sunnah rak'ahs before it.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 725 (the two rak'ahs before fajr are better than the world and what is in it)
Sahih al-Bukhari 757 (the order of the prayer taught to the man who prayed badly)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3370 (blessings on the Prophet and on Ibrahim)
